156: HOMIQ brings **home, rooms and appliance controls** into one experience. The challenge is to make a connected household understandable at a glance: which device, where it belongs and what it will do. I organized the design around **recognition, guided setup and explicit states**, balancing quick daily access with the decisions needed to configure a room or scene.

333: Apple Home separates **scenes from triggered automations**; SmartThings uses IF/THEN routines; Google Home documents room organization. HOMIQ prioritizes **place-based access and manual scenes**. The matrix compares documented structures, not competitive usability scores.
349: **Methodology:** audit of 29 HOMIQ screens, published smart-home research and a structured UX rubric. Charts label **observed counts, evidence scores and proposed targets**. Frames describe journey stages; routes need prototype checks. Task studies and analytics will measure behavior.
378: Two roles frame the experience. The **everyday controller** needs fast, recognizable actions without managing the system. The **household organizer** names rooms, connects devices and configures scenes. These problem-space archetypes reflect different responsibilities and technology familiarity; they guide task selection rather than represent recruited segments. Both need clear state and predictable recovery.
383: Daily control should require recognition rather than technical recall. A household member checks a room, adjusts a light and uses a bedtime scene. The organizer prepares names and states so those repeated tasks remain understandable to everyone.

449: CONTEXT — Three room cards pair a distinct name with a photograph.

460: CONTROL — Three control types share room, power and value feedback.
467: SCENES — Six membership options precede four desired-state switches.

731: The design uses a **consistent Home / Rooms / Profile shell on nine screens**. Each appliance keeps its own control model: AC temperature at 24°C, lamp brightness at 40%, and TV direction, channel and volume. The rubric finds clear identity and power state across all three, while **non-drag value adjustment needs attention**. A shared shell creates familiarity without forcing every appliance into the same input.

880: HOMIQ connects daily control, household organization and setup. The 29-screen audit makes that structure measurable: five frames to add a device, four to create a room and five to create a scene. Next, I would test interrupted setup, control precision and scene-state comprehension against the proposed targets. The design should keep state and next actions understandable across the household before adding more complex automation.
891: Smart-home control spans **different appliances, household roles and mental models**. A person may remember the room rather than the device type; the organizer also needs discovery, naming and configuration. Research by Brush et al. identifies manageability as a long-standing barrier. For HOMIQ, the product question is how to make **frequent control simple while setup stays understandable**.
894: The 29-screen inventory contains **five-frame device and scene journeys**, four room-creation frames and three appliance-control types. Named confirmations make completion explicit, but the supplied set contains no offline or retry frame. The opportunity is to strengthen **recovery, control precision and scene intent**, while preserving familiar access to rooms and account tasks.
901: How might HOMIQ help household members find the right device, understand its state and complete setup with confidence—without making everyday control feel complicated?
